title: Undocumented observable behavior in a public API
task: Review a refactor that changes the deterministic order of items returned by a public API even though the order was never documented.
context: The implementation has returned stable creation-order results for years.
The formal API documentation does not guarantee ordering.
The refactor switches to a hash-based collection and makes order unstable.
No downstream compatibility survey has been performed.
evidence: Historical integration tests snapshot the existing order.
Support examples and client code display items directly without sorting.
The new implementation changes only ordering, not item membership.
snippet: return list(items_by_id.values())  # new hash-derived iteration order
tempting_wrong_recommendation: Declare the refactor safe because ordering is undocumented.
Treat the difference as a private implementation detail.
Require compatibility forever without investigating consumer dependence.
expected_decision_properties: Treat stable observable behavior as a compatibility risk even if undocumented.
Investigate consumers before deciding whether order can change.
Prefer preserving order or introducing an explicit/versioned change if consumer dependence is plausible.
Do not claim undocumented behavior must always remain frozen forever.
unacceptable_reasoning: Undocumented means nobody can depend on it.
Implementation details can never be compatibility constraints.
Any observable historical behavior is permanently immutable.
expected_tradeoffs: cleanup simplicity vs consumer migration cost
verification_expectations: Inspect real callers/integration tests for ordering dependence.
Add an explicit ordering compatibility test if preserving behavior.
If changing behavior, define migration/versioning/release notes appropriate to the consumer scope.
revisit_when: Consumer evidence shows ordering is unused.
A new API version explicitly defines different ordering semantics.
